title: The Computer That Helped Win World War II
content_html:
One summer day in 1941, a British radio operator was monitoring German military frequencies and heard something unexpected in her headphones. A later report called it “strange new music.” Sounding unlike the familiar Morse dit-dit-dah of enciphered messages sent over the German Enigma network, the “new music” was a rhythmic warble of binary teletype code being transmitted at high speed.

Germany’s wartime engineers had developed a radically new encryption and transmission system. It was way more advanced than Enigma, which was patented in 1920.

To break the complex new cipher, engineer Tommy Flowers built Colossus, the world’s first large-scale programmable electronic digital computer. Flowers previously built Enigma-related codebreaking equipment for Alan Turing, the British mathematician.

Colossus was installed in the British codebreaking headquarters at Bletchley Park, about 80 kilometers from London. The room-size machine weighed around a tonne.

The computer is being commemorated as an IEEE Milestone. The dedication ceremony is scheduled to be held 29 September at Bletchley Park.

Decrypting Germany’s strange new music

Britain’s top codebreakers were quickly all over the new “music” being picked up by the intercept stations. Identifying it as encrypted teletype code was the easy part. The real problem was figuring out how the encryption machine worked. Its manufacturer was discovered at the end of the war: Berlin engineering firm C. Lorenz.

But in 1941, the Lorenz machine was just a black box to the British. They codenamed it “Tunny,” a British term for tuna fish. The Enigma breakers had set a precedent for using piscine codenames such as Dolphin, Lumpsucker, and Porpoise.

Enigma had three or four encrypting wheels. The codebreakers guessed that the Tunny machine also used a system of rotating wheels to encrypt messages. An important clue was that all the intercepted messages shared a curious feature: Each began with an uncoded list of 12 common German names, including Anton, Bertha, Conrad, and Dora. The codebreakers guessed that Tunny had 12 wheels and that the 12 names and their order somehow told the receiving operator which combination they should twist the wheels to before decrypting the message.

Then the British had an extraordinary piece of good fortune. John Tiltman, head of the research section at Bletchley Park, started analyzing a pair of intercepted messages, each around 1,200 characters long. Unusually, both began with the same sequence of names. The second message turned out to be a retype of the first, with minor differences in punctuation, a few abbreviations, and other small divergences. Tiltman managed to decrypt the two ciphertexts using a mixture of educated guesswork and intuition. The resulting 1,200 or so pairings of ciphertext and plaintext characters proved to be enough information to deduce the workings of the Tunny machine.

That was thanks to Bill Tutte, a quiet young codebreaker who spent weeks poring over the pairings. One day, he shyly announced to his superiors how Tunny worked. His description was uncannily accurate.

The next step in the Tunny machine’s downfall was achieved by Turing, fresh from his successes against Enigma.

Knowledge of how the Tunny machine worked was not enough to decrypt the messages. Codebreakers also required detailed information about how the wheels of the sender’s machine had been set up. There were adjustable pins around the circumference of each wheel: In one of its two possible positions, a pin would contribute a 1 to the encryption process, and in the other, a 0. The pins were reset from time to time.

The codebreakers also needed to know the wheels’ positions at the start of the message—which the German operators gave away in the list of 12 names.

Turing invented a tricky method, called “Turingery,” that enabled codebreakers to deduce the positions of the pins from nothing but intercepted ciphertext.

After that, the message could be decrypted, using the list of names and a British replica of the Tunny machine.

The basis of Turingery was a procedure that Turing introduced, called “delta-ing” (from the Greek letter delta). Also known as “differencing,” the process used “sideways” addition: To delta the four letters ABCD, you add (at the bit level) A to B, B to C, and C to D. Turing used delta-ing to reveal information about the wheels.

Tunny messages, often signed by Adolph Hitler himself, turned out to be pure gold for the Allies. The machine was used in Berlin by the Armed Forces High Command to communicate with front-line generals directing the war in the Eastern and Western theaters.

Once the system was broken, the Allies could eavesdrop on lengthy back-and-forth communications between the architects of Germany’s battle plans.

Turingery was the codebreakers’ only weapon against Tunny for a year, during which they managed to decrypt 1.5 million letters of ciphertext.

But everything changed when those helpful lists of names at the start of each message disappeared.

At the same time, Turingery was becoming less effective. Turing’s method depended on the German sender mistakenly using the same wheel settings to encrypt two differing messages. As security tightened across the Tunny network, the blunder became rarer.

Fortunately, Tutte had been at work devising a different decryption method, based on Turing’s delta-ing but taking a novel approach.

Building the Colossus computer

Tutte had found a way of deducing wheel information from ciphertext, with no list of names or blunders by the German operators required. His method made use of statistical properties of the Tunny machine itself.

At first, it wasn’t clear how to apply his statistical method, however. The Tunny breakers worked by hand. Applying Turingery to a message was like solving a monster Sudoku or crossword puzzle.

Tutte’s statistical method required scads of routine binary math, as well as a colossal amount of counting long binary sequences. If the process were done by hand, one message could take months to decrypt. What was needed was a machine to automate the process.

The first plan was to build a machine from electromagnetic relays, adding a couple of dozen vacuum tubes to speed up the counting. Electronic tubes were much faster than electromagnetic relays, which had slow-moving metal components. Problems with the circuit design bedeviled the machine’s relay-based logic unit, however.

Flowers was recommended by Turing and brought in to troubleshoot. He was on loan to Bletchley Park from the Post Office Research Station in London, where he had spent the prewar years designing experimental switching equipment involving thousands of vacuum tubes.

At the time, it was commonly believed that tubes could not be used in large numbers because each one contained a hot filament. This meant tubes were prone to sudden death. In a large installation, it would not be long before one tube blew and things stopped working properly.

Flowers discovered that switching tubes on and off stressed them, but leaving them on continuously made them more reliable than relays. He offered to build Bletchley Park a high-speed, all-electronic machine containing around 2,000 tubes.

Bletchley Park’s advisors rejected the idea, convinced that such a machine would never work reliably. But Flowers, confident of his proposed design, retreated to his London laboratory and quietly built the electronic machine that he believed the codebreakers needed. He and his small team of engineers worked day and night for 10 months to create Colossus.

In January 1944 some of his engineers showed up at Bletchley Park with the world’s first large-scale programmable electronic digital computer packed onto the back of a truck. Colossus was reassembled and functional in about two weeks, and it notched up its first German message on 5 February 1944.

The machine read the input—Tunny ciphertext—photoelectrically from a large loop of punched paper tape. The output—information about the wheels—went to a primitive printer that Flowers’ engineers had created from a manual typewriter, fitting relays to automate the keys. Once Colossus had cracked enough of the Tunny machine’s wheels, the information was passed on to the hand-breakers, who took over.

The codebreakers were astonished by Colossus.

“I don’t think they understood very clearly what I was proposing until they actually had the machine,” Flowers said in a 1977 interview. “They just couldn’t believe it!”

Colossus was described in almost loving terms in a since-declassified report written at Bletchley Park in 1945:

It is regretted that it is not possible to give an adequate idea of the fascination of a Colossus at work: its sheer bulk and apparent complexity; the fantastic speed of thin paper tape round the glittering pulleys; the childish pleasure of not-not, span, print main heading and other gadgets; the wizardry of purely mechanical decoding letter by letter (one novice thought she was being hoaxed); the uncanny action of the typewriter in printing the correct scores without and beyond human aid; the stepping of display; periods of eager expectation culminating in the sudden appearance of the longed-for score; and the strange rhythms characterizing every type of run: the stately break-in, the erratic short run, the regularity of wheel-breaking, the stolid rectangle interrupted by the wild leaps of the carriage-return, the frantic chatter of a motor run, even the ludicrous frenzy of hosts of bogus scores.

The demand for more Colossi

Bletchley Park’s managers, no longer leery of Flowers’s ideas, soon wanted additional Colossi. He finished building the second one in June 1944, days before D-Day and the Allied invasion of Europe. With 2,400 vacuum tubes—around 800 more than in Colossus I—Colossus II processed Tunny messages at an eye-watering speed of 25,000 characters per second.

Its maximized timing-pulse rate was not far short of the performance of the first Intel microprocessor chip from the 1970s, more than 30 years later.

Flowers conceded that “Colossus bore about as much resemblance to a modern computer as Stephenson’s [1829] Rocket locomotive did to the Royal Scot,” a state-of-the-art 20th-century train operating between London and Glasgow. But he emphasized that, nevertheless, Colossus “embodied all the basic features of a modern computer.” In Colossus, Flowers had pioneered clock pulses, bit-stream generators, control circuits, loops, counters, shift registers, interrupts, parallel processing, and more.

As the Allies slowly fought their way toward Germany, the Colossi poured out wheel information, and the codebreakers provided the military with an unparalleled view of German strategies, strengths, weaknesses, and tactical intentions.

Even with that mass of detailed intelligence, it took the Allies almost a year to move from Northern France to the German heartland. No one can say for sure how much longer the fighting would have lasted if the intelligence breakthrough had not occurred. But if Colossus and the codebreakers shortened the war even by only six months, the number of lives saved was in the millions.

There were 10 Colossi at Bletchley Park by the end of the war, housed in two vast, steel-frame, bombproof buildings, running day and night. Although concealed behind a thick veil of secrecy, Bletchley Park accommodated the world’s first electronic computing facility. It was directed by Max Newman, the mathematician who mentored Turing in prewar Cambridge.

I don’t think they understood very clearly what I was proposing until they actually had the machine. They just couldn’t believe it!”—Tommy Flowers

When the fighting ended, authorities decided that ultrasecrecy must be maintained, and orders were issued to break up the Colossi. Only two were spared.

“All that was left were the deep holes in the floor where the machines had stood,” Colossus operator Dorothy Du Boisson recalled in an interview for the book Colossus: The Secrets of Bletchley Park’s Codebreaking Computers. Norman Thurlow, one of Flowers’s engineers who was also interviewed, remembered being told in a staff memo that if the secrecy was ever lifted, he and his colleagues might be able to tell their grandchildren about Colossus and “the tapes that span on silver wheels.”

IEEE Milestone dedication at Bletchley Park

The Milestone plaque recognizing Colossus is to be displayed outside Block H at Bletchley Park, near Milton Keynes, England.

The plaque is to read:

Six Colossus codebreaking computers operated in this building in 1944–1945. Designed by Thomas H. Flowers of the British Post Office, they enabled deciphering of encrypted radio messages transmitted between German commands across occupied Europe, North Africa, and the Soviet Union. The resulting military intelligence saved countless lives and helped shorten World War II. As the first successful large-scale application of digital electronics to computing, Colossus anticipated subsequent computer developments.

The IEEE United Kingdom and Ireland Section sponsored the nomination.

Reviewed by the IEEE History Committee and awarded by the IEEE Board of Directors, IEEE Milestones recognize outstanding technical developments around the world that are at least 25 years old. The Milestone program is administered by the IEEE history and heritage group.

sentences.en: An important clue was that all the intercepted messages shared a curious feature: Each began with an uncoded list of 12 common German names, including Anton, Bertha, Conrad, and Dora.
sentences.zh: 一条重要线索是，所有截获的消息都有一个奇怪的特征：每条消息都以 12 个常见德国名字的未编码列表开头，包括安东、贝莎、康拉德和多拉。

sentences.en: The codebreakers guessed that Tunny had 12 wheels and that the 12 names and their order somehow told the receiving operator which combination they should twist the wheels to before decrypting the message.
sentences.zh: 密码破译者猜测金枪鱼有 12 个轮子，这 12 个名字和它们的顺序以某种方式告诉接收操作员在解密消息之前应该将轮子扭转成哪种组合。

blocks.html_en: Then the British had an extraordinary piece of good fortune. John Tiltman, head of the research section at Bletchley Park, started analyzing a pair of intercepted messages, each around 1,200 characters long. Unusually, both began with the same sequence of names. The second message turned out to be a retype of the first, with minor differences in punctuation, a few abbreviations, and other small divergences. Tiltman managed to decrypt the two ciphertexts using a mixture of educated guesswork and intuition. The resulting 1,200 or so pairings of ciphertext and plaintext characters proved to be enough information to deduce the workings of the Tunny machine.

sentences.en: Then the British had an extraordinary piece of good fortune.
sentences.zh: 英国人获得了非凡的好运。

sentences.en: John Tiltman, head of the research section at Bletchley Park, started analyzing a pair of intercepted messages, each around 1,200 characters long.
sentences.zh: 布莱切利公园研究部门负责人约翰·蒂特曼 (John Tiltman) 开始分析两条截获的消息，每条消息长度约为 1,200 个字符。

sentences.en: Unusually, both began with the same sequence of names.
sentences.zh: 不同寻常的是，两者都以相同的名字序列开头。

sentences.en: The second message turned out to be a retype of the first, with minor differences in punctuation, a few abbreviations, and other small divergences.
sentences.zh: 第二条消息是第一条消息的重新输入，在标点符号、一些缩写和其他方面有细微差别。

sentences.en: Tiltman managed to decrypt the two ciphertexts using a mixture of educated guesswork and intuition.
sentences.zh: 蒂特曼结合有根据的猜测和直觉，成功解密了两个密文。

sentences.en: The resulting 1,200 or so pairings of ciphertext and plaintext characters proved to be enough information to deduce the workings of the Tunny machine.
sentences.zh: 由此产生的大约 1,200 对密文和明文字符被证明足以推断出 Tunny 机器的工作原理。

blocks.html_en: That was thanks to Bill Tutte, a quiet young codebreaker who spent weeks poring over the pairings. One day, he shyly announced to his superiors how Tunny worked. His description was uncannily accurate.

sentences.en: That was thanks to Bill Tutte, a quiet young codebreaker who spent weeks poring over the pairings.
sentences.zh: 这要归功于比尔·塔特（Bill Tutte），一位安静的年轻密码破译者，他花了数周时间研究这些配对。

sentences.en: One day, he shyly announced to his superiors how Tunny worked.
sentences.zh: 有一天，他害羞地向上级汇报了图尼的工作方式。

sentences.en: His description was uncannily accurate.
sentences.zh: 他的描述出奇地准确。

blocks.html_en: The next step in the Tunny machine’s downfall was achieved by Turing, fresh from his successes against Enigma.

sentences.en: The next step in the Tunny machine’s downfall was achieved by Turing, fresh from his successes against Enigma.
sentences.zh: Tunny 机器垮台的下一步是由图灵完成的，他刚刚在对抗 Enigma 方面取得了成功。

blocks.html_en: Knowledge of how the Tunny machine worked was not enough to decrypt the messages. Codebreakers also required detailed information about how the wheels of the sender’s machine had been set up. There were adjustable pins around the circumference of each wheel: In one of its two possible positions, a pin would contribute a 1 to the encryption process, and in the other, a 0. The pins were reset from time to time.

sentences.en: Knowledge of how the Tunny machine worked was not enough to decrypt the messages.
sentences.zh: 了解金枪鱼机器的工作原理并不足以解密这些消息。

sentences.en: Codebreakers also required detailed information about how the wheels of the sender’s machine had been set up.
sentences.zh: 密码破译者还需要有关发送者机器的轮子如何设置的详细信息。

sentences.en: There were adjustable pins around the circumference of each wheel: In one of its two possible positions, a pin would contribute a 1 to the encryption process, and in the other, a 0.
sentences.zh: 每个轮子的圆周上都有可调节的销钉：在两个可能的位置之一，销钉将为加密过程贡献一个 1，而在另一个位置，则贡献一个 0。

sentences.en: The pins were reset from time to time.
sentences.zh: 引脚时常被重置。

blocks.html_en: The codebreakers also needed to know the wheels’ positions at the start of the message—which the German operators gave away in the list of 12 names.

sentences.en: The codebreakers also needed to know the wheels’ positions at the start of the message—which the German operators gave away in the list of 12 names.
sentences.zh: 密码破译者还需要知道消息开头的轮子位置——德国操作员在 12 个名字的列表中给出了这一点。

blocks.html_en: Turing invented a tricky method, called “Turingery,” that enabled codebreakers to deduce the positions of the pins from nothing but intercepted ciphertext.

sentences.en: Turing invented a tricky method, called “Turingery,” that enabled codebreakers to deduce the positions of the pins from nothing but intercepted ciphertext.
sentences.zh: 图灵发明了一种名为“Turingery”的棘手方法，使密码破译者能够仅从截获的密文中推断出引脚的位置。

blocks.html_en: After that, the message could be decrypted, using the list of names and a British replica of the Tunny machine.

sentences.en: After that, the message could be decrypted, using the list of names and a British replica of the Tunny machine.
sentences.zh: 之后，可以使用名单和英国 Tunny 机器的复制品来解密该消息。

blocks.html_en: The basis of Turingery was a procedure that Turing introduced, called “delta-ing” (from the Greek letter delta). Also known as “differencing,” the process used “sideways” addition: To delta the four letters ABCD, you add (at the bit level) A to B, B to C, and C to D. Turing used delta-ing to reveal information about the wheels.

sentences.en: The basis of Turingery was a procedure that Turing introduced, called “delta-ing” (from the Greek letter delta).
sentences.zh: 图林格里的基础是图灵引入的一个过程，称为“delta-ing”（来自希腊字母 delta）。

sentences.en: Also known as “differencing,” the process used “sideways” addition: To delta the four letters ABCD, you add (at the bit level) A to B, B to C, and C to D.
sentences.zh: 该过程也称为“差分”，使用“横向”加法：要对四个字母 ABCD 进行增量运算，可以（在位级别）将 A 添加到 B、将 B 添加到 C、将 C 添加到 D。

sentences.en: Turing used delta-ing to reveal information about the wheels.
sentences.zh: 图灵使用 delta-ing 来揭示有关轮子的信息。

blocks.html_en: Tunny messages, often signed by Adolph Hitler himself, turned out to be pure gold for the Allies. The machine was used in Berlin by the Armed Forces High Command to communicate with front-line generals directing the war in the Eastern and Western theaters.

sentences.en: Tunny messages, often signed by Adolph Hitler himself, turned out to be pure gold for the Allies.
sentences.zh: 通常由阿道夫·希特勒本人签署的金枪鱼信息对盟军来说是纯金。

sentences.en: The machine was used in Berlin by the Armed Forces High Command to communicate with front-line generals directing the war in the Eastern and Western theaters.
sentences.zh: 柏林武装部队最高指挥部使用该机器与指挥东部和西部战区战争的前线将军进行通信。

blocks.html_en: Once the system was broken, the Allies could eavesdrop on lengthy back-and-forth communications between the architects of Germany’s battle plans.

sentences.en: Once the system was broken, the Allies could eavesdrop on lengthy back-and-forth communications between the architects of Germany’s battle plans.
sentences.zh: 一旦系统被破坏，盟军就可以窃听德国作战计划的制定者之间漫长的来回通信。

blocks.html_en: Turingery was the codebreakers’ only weapon against Tunny for a year, during which they managed to decrypt 1.5 million letters of ciphertext.

sentences.en: Turingery was the codebreakers’ only weapon against Tunny for a year, during which they managed to decrypt 1.5 million letters of ciphertext.
sentences.zh: Turingery 是密码破译者一年来对抗 Tunny 的唯一武器，在此期间他们成功解密了 150 万个密文字母。

blocks.html_en: But everything changed when those helpful lists of names at the start of each message disappeared.

sentences.en: But everything changed when those helpful lists of names at the start of each message disappeared.
sentences.zh: 但当每条消息开头那些有用的姓名列表消失后，一切都改变了。

blocks.html_en: At the same time, Turingery was becoming less effective. Turing’s method depended on the German sender mistakenly using the same wheel settings to encrypt two differing messages. As security tightened across the Tunny network, the blunder became rarer.

sentences.en: At the same time, Turingery was becoming less effective.
sentences.zh: 与此同时，图林格里的效率正在下降。

sentences.en: Turing’s method depended on the German sender mistakenly using the same wheel settings to encrypt two differing messages.
sentences.zh: 图灵的方法依赖于德国发送者错误地使用相同的轮设置来加密两个不同的消息。

sentences.en: As security tightened across the Tunny network, the blunder became rarer.
sentences.zh: 随着 Tunny 网络安全措施的加强，错误变得越来越少。

blocks.html_en: Fortunately, Tutte had been at work devising a different decryption method, based on Turing’s delta-ing but taking a novel approach.

sentences.en: Fortunately, Tutte had been at work devising a different decryption method, based on Turing’s delta-ing but taking a novel approach.
sentences.zh: 幸运的是，图特一直在设计一种不同的解密方法，该方法基于图灵的 delta-ing，但采用了一种新颖的方法。

blocks.html_en: Building the Colossus computer

sentences.en: Building the Colossus computer
sentences.zh: 建造 Colossus 计算机

blocks.html_en: Tutte had found a way of deducing wheel information from ciphertext, with no list of names or blunders by the German operators required. His method made use of statistical properties of the Tunny machine itself.

sentences.en: Tutte had found a way of deducing wheel information from ciphertext, with no list of names or blunders by the German operators required.
sentences.zh: 图特找到了一种从密文中推断车轮信息的方法，不需要德国操作员列出姓名或错误。

sentences.en: His method made use of statistical properties of the Tunny machine itself.
sentences.zh: 他的方法利用了 Tunny 机器本身的统计特性。

blocks.html_en: At first, it wasn’t clear how to apply his statistical method, however. The Tunny breakers worked by hand. Applying Turingery to a message was like solving a monster Sudoku or crossword puzzle.

sentences.en: At first, it wasn’t clear how to apply his statistical method, however.
sentences.zh: 然而，一开始并不清楚如何应用他的统计方法。

sentences.en: The Tunny breakers worked by hand.
sentences.zh: 金枪鱼破碎机是手工操作的。

sentences.en: Applying Turingery to a message was like solving a monster Sudoku or crossword puzzle.
sentences.zh: 将图林格里应用于消息就像解决怪物数独或填字游戏一样。

blocks.html_en: Tutte’s statistical method required scads of routine binary math, as well as a colossal amount of counting long binary sequences. If the process were done by hand, one message could take months to decrypt. What was needed was a machine to automate the process.

sentences.en: Tutte’s statistical method required scads of routine binary math, as well as a colossal amount of counting long binary sequences.
sentences.zh: 图特的统计方法需要大量常规二进制数学，以及大量的长二进制序列计数。

sentences.en: If the process were done by hand, one message could take months to decrypt.
sentences.zh: 如果这个过程是手工完成的，一条消息可能需要几个月的时间才能解密。

sentences.en: What was needed was a machine to automate the process.
sentences.zh: 我们需要一台机器来自动化该过程。

blocks.html_en: Engineer Thomas H. Flowers developed Colossus to break a complex new German cipher.Pictorial Press/Alamy

sentences.en: Engineer Thomas H.
sentences.zh: 工程师托马斯·H.

sentences.en: Flowers developed Colossus to break a complex new German cipher.Pictorial Press/Alamy
sentences.zh: Flowers 开发了 Colossus 来破解复杂的新德国密码。Pictorial Press/Alamy

blocks.html_en: The first plan was to build a machine from electromagnetic relays, adding a couple of dozen vacuum tubes to speed up the counting. Electronic tubes were much faster than electromagnetic relays, which had slow-moving metal components. Problems with the circuit design bedeviled the machine’s relay-based logic unit, however.

sentences.en: The first plan was to build a machine from electromagnetic relays, adding a couple of dozen vacuum tubes to speed up the counting.
sentences.zh: 第一个计划是用电磁继电器制造一台机器，添加几十个真空管以加快计数速度。

sentences.en: Electronic tubes were much faster than electromagnetic relays, which had slow-moving metal components.
sentences.zh: 电子管比电磁继电器快得多，电磁继电器具有缓慢移动的金属部件。

sentences.en: Problems with the circuit design bedeviled the machine’s relay-based logic unit, however.
sentences.zh: 然而，电路设计的问题困扰着机器基于继电器的逻辑单元。

blocks.html_en: Flowers was recommended by Turing and brought in to troubleshoot. He was on loan to Bletchley Park from the Post Office Research Station in London, where he had spent the prewar years designing experimental switching equipment involving thousands of vacuum tubes.

sentences.en: Flowers was recommended by Turing and brought in to troubleshoot.
sentences.zh: 弗劳尔斯是图灵推荐的，并请来解决问题。

sentences.en: He was on loan to Bletchley Park from the Post Office Research Station in London, where he had spent the prewar years designing experimental switching equipment involving thousands of vacuum tubes.
sentences.zh: 他是从伦敦邮局研究站借调到布莱切利公园的，战前几年他在那里设计了涉及数千个真空管的实验性开关设备。

blocks.html_en: At the time, it was commonly believed that tubes could not be used in large numbers because each one contained a hot filament. This meant tubes were prone to sudden death. In a large installation, it would not be long before one tube blew and things stopped working properly.

sentences.en: At the time, it was commonly believed that tubes could not be used in large numbers because each one contained a hot filament.
sentences.zh: 当时，人们普遍认为电子管不能大量使用，因为每个电子管都含有一根热灯丝。

sentences.en: This meant tubes were prone to sudden death.
sentences.zh: 这意味着管子很容易突然死亡。

sentences.en: In a large installation, it would not be long before one tube blew and things stopped working properly.
sentences.zh: 在大型装置中，过不了多久，一根管子就会爆炸，一切都会停止正常工作。

blocks.html_en: Flowers discovered that switching tubes on and off stressed them, but leaving them on continuously made them more reliable than relays. He offered to build Bletchley Park a high-speed, all-electronic machine containing around 2,000 tubes.

sentences.en: Flowers discovered that switching tubes on and off stressed them, but leaving them on continuously made them more reliable than relays.
sentences.zh: 弗劳尔斯发现，打开和关闭电子管会给它们带来压力，但让它们持续打开会让它们比继电器更可靠。

sentences.en: He offered to build Bletchley Park a high-speed, all-electronic machine containing around 2,000 tubes.
sentences.zh: 他提议为布莱切利公园建造一台包含大约 2,000 个管子的高速全电子机器。

blocks.html_en: Bletchley Park’s advisors rejected the idea, convinced that such a machine would never work reliably. But Flowers, confident of his proposed design, retreated to his London laboratory and quietly built the electronic machine that he believed the codebreakers needed. He and his small team of engineers worked day and night for 10 months to create Colossus.

sentences.en: Bletchley Park’s advisors rejected the idea, convinced that such a machine would never work reliably.
sentences.zh: 布莱切利公园的顾问拒绝了这个想法，认为这样的机器永远无法可靠地工作。

sentences.en: But Flowers, confident of his proposed design, retreated to his London laboratory and quietly built the electronic machine that he believed the codebreakers needed.
sentences.zh: 但弗劳尔斯对他提出的设计充满信心，他回到伦敦实验室，悄悄建造了他认为密码破译者需要的电子机器。

sentences.en: He and his small team of engineers worked day and night for 10 months to create Colossus.
sentences.zh: 他和他的工程师小团队夜以继日地工作了 10 个月才创建了 Colossus。

blocks.html_en: In January 1944 some of his engineers showed up at Bletchley Park with the world’s first large-scale programmable electronic digital computer packed onto the back of a truck. Colossus was reassembled and functional in about two weeks, and it notched up its first German message on 5 February 1944.

sentences.en: In January 1944 some of his engineers showed up at Bletchley Park with the world’s first large-scale programmable electronic digital computer packed onto the back of a truck.
sentences.zh: 1944 年 1 月，他的一些工程师出现在布莱奇利公园，他们的卡车后面装着世界上第一台大型可编程电子数字计算机。

sentences.en: Colossus was reassembled and functional in about two weeks, and it notched up its first German message on 5 February 1944.
sentences.zh: Colossus 在大约两周内重新组装完毕并投入使用，并于 1944 年 2 月 5 日发出了第一条德国信息。

blocks.html_en: The machine read the input—Tunny ciphertext—photoelectrically from a large loop of punched paper tape. The output—information about the wheels—went to a primitive printer that Flowers’ engineers had created from a manual typewriter, fitting relays to automate the keys. Once Colossus had cracked enough of the Tunny machine’s wheels, the information was passed on to the hand-breakers, who took over.

sentences.en: The machine read the input—Tunny ciphertext—photoelectrically from a large loop of punched paper tape.
sentences.zh: 机器以光电方式从一大圈打孔纸带上读取输入——金枪鱼密文。

sentences.en: The output—information about the wheels—went to a primitive printer that Flowers’ engineers had created from a manual typewriter, fitting relays to automate the keys.
sentences.zh: 输出——有关车轮的信息——被传送到弗劳尔斯的工程师用手动打字机创建的一台原始打印机，安装继电器以实现按键自动化。

sentences.en: Once Colossus had cracked enough of the Tunny machine’s wheels, the information was passed on to the hand-breakers, who took over.
sentences.zh: 一旦巨像对金枪鱼机器的轮子进行了足够的破解，信息就会传递给破解者，然后由后者接管。

blocks.html_en: The codebreakers were astonished by Colossus.

sentences.en: The codebreakers were astonished by Colossus.
sentences.zh: 密码破译者对巨像感到惊讶。

blocks.html_en: “I don’t think they understood very clearly what I was proposing until they actually had the machine,” Flowers said in a 1977 interview. “They just couldn’t believe it!”

sentences.en: “I don’t think they understood very clearly what I was proposing until they actually had the machine,” Flowers said in a 1977 interview.
sentences.zh: “我认为，在他们真正拥有这台机器之前，他们并没有非常清楚地理解我的提议，”弗劳尔斯在 1977 年的一次采访中说道。

sentences.en: “They just couldn’t believe it!”
sentences.zh: “他们简直不敢相信！”

blocks.html_en: Colossus was described in almost loving terms in a since-declassified report written at Bletchley Park in 1945:

sentences.en: Colossus was described in almost loving terms in a since-declassified report written at Bletchley Park in 1945:
sentences.zh: 1945 年在布莱切利公园撰写的一份现已解密的报告中，对 Colossus 的描述近乎充满爱意：

blocks.html_en: It is regretted that it is not possible to give an adequate idea of the fascination of a Colossus at work: its sheer bulk and apparent complexity; the fantastic speed of thin paper tape round the glittering pulleys; the childish pleasure of not-not, span, print main heading and other gadgets; the wizardry of purely mechanical decoding letter by letter (one novice thought she was being hoaxed); the uncanny action of the typewriter in printing the correct scores without and beyond human aid; the stepping of display; periods of eager expectation culminating in the sudden appearance of the longed-for score; and the strange rhythms characterizing every type of run: the stately break-in, the erratic short run, the regularity of wheel-breaking, the stolid rectangle interrupted by the wild leaps of the carriage-return, the frantic chatter of a motor run, even the ludicrous frenzy of hosts of bogus scores.

sentences.en: It is regretted that it is not possible to give an adequate idea of the fascination of a Colossus at work: its sheer bulk and apparent complexity; the fantastic speed of thin paper tape round the glittering pulleys; the childish pleasure of not-not, span, print main heading and other gadgets; the wizardry of purely mechanical decoding letter by letter (one novice thought she was being hoaxed); the uncanny action of the typewriter in printing the correct scores without and beyond human aid; the stepping of display; periods of eager expectation culminating in the sudden appearance of the longed-for score; and the strange rhythms characterizing every type of run: the stately break-in, the erratic short run, the regularity of wheel-breaking, the stolid rectangle interrupted by the wild leaps of the carriage-return, the frantic chatter of a motor run, even the ludicrous frenzy of hosts of bogus scores.
sentences.zh: 令人遗憾的是，我们无法充分了解巨像在工作中的魅力：其庞大的体积和明显的复杂性；薄纸带绕着闪闪发光的滑轮的惊人速度； not-not、span、打印主标题和其他小工具的幼稚乐趣；纯机械逐字解码的魔法（一位新手认为她被骗了）；打字机在没有人类帮助的情况下打印出正确的乐谱的不可思议的动作；显示的步进；热切期待的时期，最终以期盼已久的乐谱突然出现而达到顶峰；每种类型的跑步都具有奇怪的节奏：庄严的磨合，不稳定的短跑，轮子损坏的规律性，被回车的疯狂跳跃打断的冷漠矩形，马达运行的疯狂喋喋不休，甚至是大量伪造乐谱的可笑疯狂。

blocks.html_en: The demand for more Colossi

sentences.en: The demand for more Colossi
sentences.zh: 对更多 Colossi 的需求

blocks.html_en: Bletchley Park’s managers, no longer leery of Flowers’s ideas, soon wanted additional Colossi. He finished building the second one in June 1944, days before D-Day and the Allied invasion of Europe. With 2,400 vacuum tubes—around 800 more than in Colossus I—Colossus II processed Tunny messages at an eye-watering speed of 25,000 characters per second.

sentences.en: Bletchley Park’s managers, no longer leery of Flowers’s ideas, soon wanted additional Colossi.
sentences.zh: 布莱切利公园的经理们不再对弗劳尔斯的想法持怀疑态度，很快就想要更多的巨像。

sentences.en: He finished building the second one in June 1944, days before D-Day and the Allied invasion of Europe.
sentences.zh: 1944 年 6 月，即诺曼底登陆日和盟军入侵欧洲的前几天，他完成了第二艘飞机的建造。

sentences.en: With 2,400 vacuum tubes—around 800 more than in Colossus I—Colossus II processed Tunny messages at an eye-watering speed of 25,000 characters per second.
sentences.zh: Colossus II 拥有 2,400 个真空管（比 Colossus I 多出大约 800 个），以每秒 25,000 个字符的惊人速度处理 Tunny 消息。

content_html_zh:
1941 年的一个夏日，一位英国无线电操作员正在监听德国军用频率，并在她的耳机中听到了一些意想不到的声音。 后来的一份报告称其为“奇怪的新音乐”。 听起来不像通过德国恩尼格玛网络发送的熟悉的莫尔斯电报加密信息，“新音乐”是高速传输的二进制电传打字机代码的有节奏的颤音。

德国战时工程师开发了一种全新的加密和传输系统。 它比 1920 年获得专利的 Enigma 先进得多。

为了破解复杂的新密码，工程师 Tommy Flowers 建造了 Colossus，世界上第一台大规模可编程电子数字计算机。 弗劳尔斯此前曾为英国数学家阿兰·图灵建造过与 Enigma 相关的密码破译设备。

Colossus 安装在距离伦敦约 80 公里的布莱切利公园的英国密码破译总部。 这台房间大小的机器重约一吨。

该计算机被作为 IEEE 里程碑进行纪念。 落成仪式定于 9 月 29 日在布莱切利公园举行。

解密德国奇怪的新音乐

英国顶尖的密码破译者很快就被拦截站捕捉到的新“音乐”所吸引。 将其识别为加密的电传打字机代码是比较容易的部分。 真正的问题是弄清楚加密机是如何工作的。 其制造商在战争结束时被发现：柏林工程公司 C. 洛伦兹。

但在 1941 年，洛伦兹机对英国人来说还只是一个黑匣子。 他们将其代号为“Tunny”，这是英国对金枪鱼的称呼。 谜团破解者开创了使用海豚、Lumpsucker 和 Porpoise 等鱼类代号的先例。

Enigma 有三四个加密轮。 密码破译者猜测金枪鱼机器还使用旋转轮系统来加密消息。 一条重要线索是，所有截获的消息都有一个奇怪的特征：每条消息都以 12 个常见德国名字的未编码列表开头，包括安东、贝莎、康拉德和多拉。 密码破译者猜测金枪鱼有 12 个轮子，这 12 个名字和它们的顺序以某种方式告诉接收操作员在解密消息之前应该将轮子扭转成哪种组合。

英国人获得了非凡的好运。 布莱切利公园研究部门负责人约翰·蒂特曼 (John Tiltman) 开始分析两条截获的消息，每条消息长度约为 1,200 个字符。 不同寻常的是，两者都以相同的名字序列开头。 第二条消息是第一条消息的重新输入，在标点符号、一些缩写和其他方面有细微差别。 蒂特曼结合有根据的猜测和直觉，成功解密了两个密文。 由此产生的大约 1,200 对密文和明文字符被证明足以推断出 Tunny 机器的工作原理。

这要归功于比尔·塔特（Bill Tutte），一位安静的年轻密码破译者，他花了数周时间研究这些配对。 有一天，他害羞地向上级汇报了图尼的工作方式。 他的描述出奇地准确。

Tunny 机器垮台的下一步是由图灵完成的，他刚刚在对抗 Enigma 方面取得了成功。

了解金枪鱼机器的工作原理并不足以解密这些消息。 密码破译者还需要有关发送者机器的轮子如何设置的详细信息。 每个轮子的圆周上都有可调节的销钉：在两个可能的位置之一，销钉将为加密过程贡献一个 1，而在另一个位置，则贡献一个 0。 引脚时常被重置。

密码破译者还需要知道消息开头的轮子位置——德国操作员在 12 个名字的列表中给出了这一点。

图灵发明了一种名为“Turingery”的棘手方法，使密码破译者能够仅从截获的密文中推断出引脚的位置。

之后，可以使用名单和英国 Tunny 机器的复制品来解密该消息。

图林格里的基础是图灵引入的一个过程，称为“delta-ing”（来自希腊字母 delta）。 该过程也称为“差分”，使用“横向”加法：要对四个字母 ABCD 进行增量运算，可以（在位级别）将 A 添加到 B、将 B 添加到 C、将 C 添加到 D。 图灵使用 delta-ing 来揭示有关轮子的信息。

通常由阿道夫·希特勒本人签署的金枪鱼信息对盟军来说是纯金。 柏林武装部队最高指挥部使用该机器与指挥东部和西部战区战争的前线将军进行通信。

一旦系统被破坏，盟军就可以窃听德国作战计划的制定者之间漫长的来回通信。

Turingery 是密码破译者一年来对抗 Tunny 的唯一武器，在此期间他们成功解密了 150 万个密文字母。

但当每条消息开头那些有用的姓名列表消失后，一切都改变了。

与此同时，图林格里的效率正在下降。 图灵的方法依赖于德国发送者错误地使用相同的轮设置来加密两个不同的消息。 随着 Tunny 网络安全措施的加强，错误变得越来越少。

幸运的是，图特一直在设计一种不同的解密方法，该方法基于图灵的 delta-ing，但采用了一种新颖的方法。

建造 Colossus 计算机

图特找到了一种从密文中推断车轮信息的方法，不需要德国操作员列出姓名或错误。 他的方法利用了 Tunny 机器本身的统计特性。

然而，一开始并不清楚如何应用他的统计方法。 金枪鱼破碎机是手工操作的。 将图林格里应用于消息就像解决怪物数独或填字游戏一样。

图特的统计方法需要大量常规二进制数学，以及大量的长二进制序列计数。 如果这个过程是手工完成的，一条消息可能需要几个月的时间才能解密。 我们需要一台机器来自动化该过程。

工程师托马斯·H. Flowers 开发了 Colossus 来破解复杂的新德国密码。Pictorial Press/Alamy

第一个计划是用电磁继电器制造一台机器，添加几十个真空管以加快计数速度。 电子管比电磁继电器快得多，电磁继电器具有缓慢移动的金属部件。 然而，电路设计的问题困扰着机器基于继电器的逻辑单元。

弗劳尔斯是图灵推荐的，并请来解决问题。 他是从伦敦邮局研究站借调到布莱切利公园的，战前几年他在那里设计了涉及数千个真空管的实验性开关设备。

当时，人们普遍认为电子管不能大量使用，因为每个电子管都含有一根热灯丝。 这意味着管子很容易突然死亡。 在大型装置中，过不了多久，一根管子就会爆炸，一切都会停止正常工作。

弗劳尔斯发现，打开和关闭电子管会给它们带来压力，但让它们持续打开会让它们比继电器更可靠。 他提议为布莱切利公园建造一台包含大约 2,000 个管子的高速全电子机器。

布莱切利公园的顾问拒绝了这个想法，认为这样的机器永远无法可靠地工作。 但弗劳尔斯对他提出的设计充满信心，他回到伦敦实验室，悄悄建造了他认为密码破译者需要的电子机器。 他和他的工程师小团队夜以继日地工作了 10 个月才创建了 Colossus。

1944 年 1 月，他的一些工程师出现在布莱奇利公园，他们的卡车后面装着世界上第一台大型可编程电子数字计算机。 Colossus 在大约两周内重新组装完毕并投入使用，并于 1944 年 2 月 5 日发出了第一条德国信息。

机器以光电方式从一大圈打孔纸带上读取输入——金枪鱼密文。 输出——有关车轮的信息——被传送到弗劳尔斯的工程师用手动打字机创建的一台原始打印机，安装继电器以实现按键自动化。 一旦巨像对金枪鱼机器的轮子进行了足够的破解，信息就会传递给破解者，然后由后者接管。

密码破译者对巨像感到惊讶。

“我认为，在他们真正拥有这台机器之前，他们并没有非常清楚地理解我的提议，”弗劳尔斯在 1977 年的一次采访中说道。 “他们简直不敢相信！”

1945 年在布莱切利公园撰写的一份现已解密的报告中，对 Colossus 的描述近乎充满爱意：

令人遗憾的是，我们无法充分了解巨像在工作中的魅力：其庞大的体积和明显的复杂性；薄纸带绕着闪闪发光的滑轮的惊人速度； not-not、span、打印主标题和其他小工具的幼稚乐趣；纯机械逐字解码的魔法（一位新手认为她被骗了）；打字机在没有人类帮助的情况下打印出正确的乐谱的不可思议的动作；显示的步进；热切期待的时期，最终以期盼已久的乐谱突然出现而达到顶峰；每种类型的跑步都具有奇怪的节奏：庄严的磨合，不稳定的短跑，轮子损坏的规律性，被回车的疯狂跳跃打断的冷漠矩形，马达运行的疯狂喋喋不休，甚至是大量伪造乐谱的可笑疯狂。

对更多 Colossi 的需求

布莱切利公园的经理们不再对弗劳尔斯的想法持怀疑态度，很快就想要更多的巨像。 1944 年 6 月，即诺曼底登陆日和盟军入侵欧洲的前几天，他完成了第二艘飞机的建造。 Colossus II 拥有 2,400 个真空管（比 Colossus I 多出大约 800 个），以每秒 25,000 个字符的惊人速度处理 Tunny 消息。

其最大定时脉冲率与 30 多年后 20 世纪 70 年代首款英特尔微处理器芯片的性能相差不远。

弗劳尔斯承认，“Colossus 与现代计算机的相似度就像斯蒂芬森 (Stephenson) [1829] 的火箭机车与皇家苏格兰号 (Royal Scot) 的相似之处”，皇家苏格兰号是运行在伦敦和格拉斯哥之间的最先进的 20 世纪火车。 但他强调，尽管如此，Colossus“体现了现代计算机的所有基本特征”。 在 Colossus 中，弗劳尔斯开创了时钟脉冲、比特流生成器、控制电路、循环、计数器、移位寄存器、中断、并行处理等。

当盟军慢慢向德国推进时，巨像倾泻出轮盘信息，密码破译者为军队提供了关于德国战略、优势、劣势和战术意图的无与伦比的视角。

即使掌握了大量详细情报，盟军还是花了将近一年的时间才从法国北部转移到德国腹地。 没有人能确切地说，如果情报没有突破，战斗还会持续多久。 但即使巨像和密码破译者将战争缩短了六个月，也能挽救数百万人的生命。

战争结束时，布莱奇利公园里有 10 座巨像，它们被安置在两座巨大的钢架防弹建筑中，日夜运转。 尽管隐藏在厚厚的秘密面纱后面，布莱奇利公园还是世界上第一个电子计算设施。 它的导演是马克斯·纽曼（Max Newman），他是战前在剑桥指导图灵的数学家。

战斗结束后，当局决定必须保持高度机密，并下令拆散巨像。 只有两人幸免于难。

“剩下的只是机器所在的地板上的深洞，”Colossus 操作员多萝西·杜布瓦森 (Dorothy Du Boisson) 在接受《Colossus：布莱奇利公园密码破译计算机的秘密》一书的采访时回忆道。 诺曼·瑟洛（Norman Thurlow）是弗劳尔斯公司的一名工程师，他也接受了采访，他记得在一份员工备忘录中被告知，如果保密被解除，他和他的同事们也许能够向他们的孙子们讲述巨像和“跨在银轮上的磁带”。
